title: Validate JSON Route Handler requests without leaking exceptions
businessContext: Review a focused Next.js application change before it reaches production. The proposed file below contains the defect or unsupported assumption; external application services, where imported, are integration boundaries.
problemStatement: Review the proposed app/api/notes/route.ts change. Identify the incorrect framework assumption, propose a minimal corrected implementation, and provide evidence for the selected version scope and its 15/16 differences. Explain the interview variation after solving the base task. This is a framework code review: actual rendering, routing and cache behavior must be checked in a real Next.js build, not a browser function sandbox.
starterCode: export async function POST(request:Request){const body=await request.json();return Response.json({title:body.title.trim()});}

codeReviewFiles.newCode: export async function POST(request:Request){const body=await request.json();return Response.json({title:body.title.trim()});}

constraints: Preserve the stated user behavior and keep trust boundaries explicit.
Use the selected version’s documented API; do not suppress build/type failures to hide the defect.
Send missing/wrong content type, invalid JSON, null and a valid title.
Enforce body-size limits at the receiving server/deployment boundary.
Add an authenticated persistence integration and verify transaction failures separately.
candidateTasks: Add actionable line-level review comments explaining impact and correction.
Write the corrected file in the local IDE copy; split annotated companion files where instructed.
Record actual build/request/navigation evidence against the acceptance checks and compare version notes.
hints: A TypeScript expectation does not validate an HTTP body.
Send missing/wrong content type, invalid JSON, null and a valid title.
alternativeApproaches: Publish a schema with status/error shapes and use contract tests. Bound reads before parsing large bodies, and avoid claiming that a Content-Length header alone enforces a trustworthy size limit.
commonMistakes: Verifying only next dev when the behavior depends on production rendering or bundling.
Treating a visible UI state, matcher or TypeScript type as a substitute for server-side validation and authorization.
